stops.name: Lava Beds, Modoc War: the camera at the front
stops.campa: In the spring of 1873 Muybridge carries his flying studio to the Modoc War in the volcanic lava beds of northern California, where Captain Jack's band holds the black stone fortress against the U.S. Army. He photographs the soldiers, the Warm Springs scouts, the desolate battlefield of cinders. These are among the first photographs made near an active American Indian war. Between the horse trials, the artist of arrested motion turns his lens on history caught mid-stride: an army bogged in lava, a people at the end of their ground.

stops.name: San Francisco: the discovery in the photographer's house
stops.campa: In October 1874 Muybridge finds, tucked with a photograph of his infant son Florado, a note in Flora's hand and the child's name written as 'Little Harry.' He confronts the midwife, who lets slip that the drama critic Major Harry Larkyns, charming, penniless, a fixture of the theatres, has been the young wife's lover, and may be the boy's true father. The betrayed husband, already a man remade by a blow to the skull, goes cold and deliberate. He takes his revolver, learns where Larkyns is, and boards the boat north. He tells no one to stop him.

stops.name: Yellow Jacket Mine, near Calistoga: the killing of Harry Larkyns
stops.campa: On the night of 17 October 1874 Muybridge comes by wagon and ferry to the Yellow Jacket quicksilver mine above Calistoga, where Larkyns is surveying. He knocks; a card game is in progress; Larkyns comes to the door. Muybridge speaks, then fires a single ball point-blank into the heart. Larkyns staggers out under an oak and dies within minutes. The photographer does not flee. He sits calmly among the horrified miners, tells them plainly that he has killed the man who wronged him, that men of family will understand, and that he has no regret. He waits to be taken.
stops.quote: Good evening, Major, my name is Muybridge, and here's the answer to the letter you sent my wife.
stops.quote_source: Muybridge to Harry Larkyns at the Yellow Jacket Mine, as recorded in trial testimony and biographies

stops.name: Napa Courthouse: acquitted by justifiable homicide, February 1875
stops.campa: In February 1875 Muybridge stands trial for murder at the Napa County courthouse before Judge W. W. Wallace. His counsel does not much deny the deed; he pleads the outrage of a wronged husband. Stanford quietly helps pay the defense. The judge instructs the all-male jury that the law knows no such excuse. They deliberate through the night and return, against his instruction, a verdict of not guilty: justifiable homicide. They cannot punish, they say, a man for doing what any of them would have done. At the words Muybridge breaks: he sobs, convulses, and collapses. A free man, he is spirited out of California toward the tropics.
stops.quote: If their verdict was not in accordance with the law, it was in accordance with the law of human nature.
stops.quote_source: Contemporary account of the Napa jury's reasoning, February 1875

stops.name: Panama City: the Pacific Mail exile begins
stops.campa: In February 1875, days after his acquittal, Muybridge boards a Pacific Mail steamer and leaves the scene of his ruin for a nine-month commission in Central America. He lands at the Isthmus of Panama, photographing the port, the railway across the neck of the continent, the churches and jungle of the tropics for the steamship company, which wants his pictures to lure trade and settlers. Wifeless: Flora will die that July, her small son sent to an orphanage. The exile buries himself in work, coating plates in tropical heat, inventing skies for volcanoes back home.

stops.name: Antigua, Guatemala: the coffee plantations and the volcanoes
stops.campa: For six months Muybridge works in Guatemala, his richest tropical ground, based near Antigua beneath its ring of volcanoes. He photographs the colonial ruins, the indigenous coffee-pickers of Las Nubes, the weeding and drying of the beans, the cochineal cactus, whole villages posed among the drying-yards: a portrait of an emerging coffee empire built for its investors. Back in San Francisco he will deepen these prints, painting in moonlight and cloud. Only five copies of the great album are made. Renewed, his grief worked into labor, he sails home to California and to the horse still waiting on the Palo Alto track.

stops.name: Palo Alto Stock Farm: the bank of cameras, 15 June 1878
stops.campa: On 15 June 1878, before invited turfmen and the press at Stanford's Palo Alto farm, the great experiment succeeds. Along the track a bank of twenty-four cameras faces a white wall marked in numbered lines. Threads stretched across the course run to electric shutters; as the racing mare Sallie Gardner strikes each trip-wire, the circuit breaks and the shutter fires, one after another, in a thousandth of a second. Developed on the spot, the plates show what no eye ever saw: the galloping horse, at full stretch, all four hooves gathered clear of the earth. The wager is settled. Motion has been arrested and read.
stops.quote: The Horse in Motion. 'Sallie Gardner,' owned by Leland Stanford; running at a 1.40 gait over the Palo Alto track, 19th June 1878.
stops.quote_source: Muybridge, caption to the published cabinet-card series, 1878

stops.name: San Francisco: the zoopraxiscope whirls the frozen frames to life
stops.campa: Having stopped motion, Muybridge now gives it back. In 1879 he devises the zoopraxiscope: a lantern that spins a glass disc painted with his sequenced figures past a slotted counter-wheel, so the still phases blur into one moving image thrown on a wall. On 4 May 1880, before the San Francisco Art Association, the horse gallops again on the screen; a bull charges, an athlete runs, from images built out of dead instants. The audience sees the first projected moving pictures in history. The ghost of cinema is loosed. The man who arrested the second has invented the illusion that will fill the coming century's dark theatres.

stops.name: Paris: Marey's soirée and the meeting of the motion-hunters
stops.campa: On 26 September 1881 the physiologist Étienne-Jules Marey gathers the science of Paris into his apartment at 11 Boulevard Delessert, below the Trocadéro, to meet the American who has caught the horse in the air. Muybridge whirls his zoopraxiscope before Helmholtz and the men of the laboratories; days later the painter Meissonier fills his studio on the Boulevard Malesherbes with artists to see the same marvel. Here two obsessions fuse: Muybridge, who reads the body with banks of cameras, and Marey, who will read it with a single chronophotographic gun. From this room the study of motion becomes a science, and the road runs toward the moving film.

stops.name: Royal Institution, London: the sun-picture lecture, 1882
stops.campa: In 1882 Muybridge crosses to Europe and lectures on the science of animal motion, whirling his zoopraxiscope before packed halls. At the Royal Institution in London he speaks to a sold-out audience that includes the Prince of Wales, the future Edward VII, and the great men of British science. But triumph curdles into feud: Stanford has published the horse studies under a hired doctor's name, all but erasing Muybridge, who sues and loses. The showman is celebrated across two continents and robbed of his own discovery in the same season.

stops.name: University of Pennsylvania: the great atlas of Animal Locomotion
stops.campa: From 1884 the University of Pennsylvania, urged by the painter Thomas Eakins and Provost William Pepper, gives Muybridge an outdoor studio at Thirty-sixth and Pine and banks of cameras to record the moving body. For three years he photographs everything that walks, runs, climbs, falls, throws, lifts: horses, elephants, birds, and men and women, many nude, against his numbered grid. The result, published in 1887 as Animal Locomotion, is 781 collotype plates, over twenty thousand images: a vast, strange atlas of every gait of every creature, the body dissected into its hidden instants. It is the quipu's own dream: a gallery of moving bodies, motion itself made a book.

stops.name: Chicago, Midway Plaisance: the first movie theatre, 1893
stops.campa: At the World's Columbian Exposition of 1893, on the Midway Plaisance in Chicago, Muybridge opens the Zoopraxographical Hall: a building raised for the sole purpose of showing his moving pictures to a paying public. Night after night the crowds file in, pay their coin, and watch horses gallop and dancers whirl on the screen by lantern-light. It is the first commercial motion-picture theatre in the world, two years before the Lumières' Cinématographe. The old showman, sixty-three, stands in the doorway of the whole coming age of film: the movie house begins as his sideshow on the fairground midway.
